title: Bridging Compute- and Data-Optimal Pretraining
claim: Extra compute on derived data departs from the classical frontier, but a token-effectiveness mapping collapses runs onto one line with saturating returns.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, shared loss/token axes, shaded regime regions in (a)
description: Three side-by-side plots. Panel (a) plots validation loss against fresh tokens D on log axes. A thick black compute-optimal curve sits above a red data-optimal curve. The area between them is shaded blue and labeled compute-bound. Below the red curve is a pink data-bound region, and a green model-bound floor lies beneath that. Thin teal-to-blue curves and dots of different sizes show runs that use extra compute. Panel (b) re-plots the same points against effective tokens D_eff = D + ηD'. The points collapse onto the single black classical curve, and the green model-bound floor is still marked. Panel (c) plots D_eff against total tokens trained. Purple, pink and yellow curves for model sizes 30m, 60m and 370m rise along the dashed y=x full-credit line, then plateau at saturation levels. Marker size encodes tokens per parameter. A legend sits in the top left and another in the bottom right. The eye goes first to the large panel (a) curves and the shaded regions.
caption: CD-scaling law overview. (a) For a model of size N, classical scaling laws assume 1-epoch training on fresh data, which coincides with the compute-optimal Pareto frontier. Spending additional compute on derived tokens D′ produced from D, via data expansion strategies such as multi-epoch repetition, paraphrasing, or distillation, departs from this frontier and reaches lower loss without curating more fresh data. (b) To describe training behavior beyond the compute-optimal frontier, CD-scaling laws introduce a token effectiveness function η that maps each derived token to a fresh-data equivalent. Under this mapping, runs beyond the compute-optimal frontier collapse onto the classical scaling line. (c) Both the saturation level of effective tokens and the rate of approach depend on N and TPP: as the model grows and data becomes more abundant, additional compute brings diminishing returns.
abstract: Classical compute-optimal scaling laws assume an unbounded supply of fresh pretraining data, yet pretraining is increasingly entering a regime in which compute grows faster than the availability of high-quality data. We propose Compute-Data (CD) scaling laws, a unified framework that bridges compute-optimal scaling, where data scales freely with compute, and data-optimal scaling, where the corpus is fixed while compute can grow without bound. CD scaling extends classical scaling laws by introducing a token-effectiveness function, $Î·$, which quantifies the value of a derived token-produced, for example, through multi-epoch repetition or paraphrasing-relative to a fresh token, ranging from a perfect substitute to having no value. We fit $Î·$ for two data-expansion strategies, multi-epoch repetition and paraphrasing, across model sizes from 14M to 600M parameters using the Dolma-3 corpus. We find that token effectiveness is far from constant: it depends jointly on model size, the tokens-per-parameter ratio, and the amount of derived data, and it saturates as the corpus is expanded. The functional form of $Î·$ implies diminishing returns when substituting compute for data as either model size or data availability increases. It also partitions training into three operational regimes---compute-bound, data-bound, and model-bound---and shows that classical compute-optimal allocation is suboptimal across most practically relevant settings.
